html:
Spanish Florida was Spain's colony in the American Southeast, run from St. Augustine, founded in 1565. The map shows it in 1650 and 1700, when it covered the peninsula and the coast of what is now Georgia and the Florida panhandle.

Florida was never rich. Spain held it mainly to guard the route of the treasure fleets, which sailed home past its coast through the Straits of Florida. Its real centre was a chain of Franciscan missions among the Timucua, the Guale of the Georgia coast and the Apalachee, whose people grew maize and carried loads for the colony. Revolts in 1647 and 1656 showed how heavy that burden was.

English Carolina, founded in 1670, became the great threat. Spain built the stone fort of Castillo de San Marcos at St. Augustine from 1672. In 1702 and 1704 Carolina forces and their Creek allies burned St. Augustine's town and destroyed the Apalachee missions, carrying off thousands of captives. From then on Spain held little more than its forts. For the colony's later years see Florida (Spain); Spain gave it to Britain in 1763.
